opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I find really interesting, because biomedicine is full of data that doesn't fit neatly into the text-and-images paradigm most models are built around. Think of whole genome sequences, single-cell RNA data, continuous ECG or EEG signals, 3D imaging like CT and MRI volumes, or longitudinal EHR records spanning decades. Some of these are enormous, some are very high-dimensional, and some have structure that a general-purpose tokenizer just doesn't capture well.

I think there are roughly two broad approaches, and the right answer is probably a mix of both.

The first is to make the general model natively multimodal by training it to ingest these modalities directly, usually with specialized encoders that project the data into the model's representation space. That's appealing because you get rich cross-modal reasoning. The model can look at a pathology slide, a genomic profile, and the clinical notes together and reason about them jointly. But it's expensive, you need a lot of paired data, and for some modalities the data is scarce or locked up for privacy reasons.

The second approach, which I think is underrated, is to treat the general model as an orchestrator, an agent that uses tools. There are already excellent specialized models and pipelines for things like variant calling, protein structure prediction, or analyzing particular imaging types. Rather than forcing everything into one set of weights, you let the language model call those tools, interpret the outputs, write and run analysis code, and integrate the results into its reasoning. This plays to what large models are already good at: planning, synthesis, and communicating with clinicians and researchers in natural language.

In practice, I'd say the near-term path is heavily tool-based, because it's more modular, easier to validate, and you can swap in better specialized components as they emerge. Over time, as we get more data and better encoders, I'd expect more of these modalities to be absorbed natively, especially the ones where joint reasoning really matters.

Whichever way you go, the bar for evaluation has to be high. In medicine, it's not enough for a model to produce a plausible-sounding interpretation. You need to know when it's grounded in the actual data versus pattern-matching on the surrounding text. So investing in rigorous, modality-specific evaluation, and building models that are transparent about uncertainty and about what they did or didn't actually look at, is just as important as the ingestion question itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something we think about a lot. The honest answer is that a lot of the most important biomedical data just doesn't look like text or natural images. You've got genomics, you've got high-resolution histopathology slides that are gigapixel-scale, you've got time-series like ECG and continuous glucose monitoring, you've got 3D volumetric imaging like CT and MRI. Each of these has its own structure, and if you try to force them through a vanilla language model or a vanilla vision encoder, you usually lose a lot.

So the way I think about it is in roughly two layers. The first is: do you need to natively ingest the raw modality at all, or can you work through tooling? For a lot of clinically relevant questions, there's already a specialized model or pipeline that does a very good job on the raw signal, and the generalist model's job is to orchestrate. Call the genomics tool, get back variant annotations, reason over them in natural language. That's a pragmatic path, and frankly it's where a lot of real-world value is right now, because the specialist models are mature and the generalist model is good at integration and communication.

The second layer is where I think the more interesting research is, which is actually extending the model's representation space to these modalities. The pattern we found works well is to train a modality-specific encoder, something that understands the native structure of the data, and then learn a relatively lightweight adapter that maps those encoder outputs into the language model's token space. You keep the core model mostly intact, so you don't lose its reasoning and medical knowledge, but now it can attend over an embedding of a pathology patch or a genomic region the same way it attends over text. We did versions of this with Med-PaLM M, and the striking thing was that a single model could move across radiology, pathology, dermatology, genomics, with performance that was competitive with specialized systems in many cases.

The thing I'd caution against is assuming that just because you can tokenize something, the model understands it. Genomics is a good example. You can feed in sequence, but the clinically meaningful signal is often very sparse and the context is enormous. So you really want to be thoughtful about what representation you're handing the model. Sometimes that means pre-processing into a structured summary, sometimes it means a learned embedding, and sometimes it means acknowledging that this isn't a problem a general-purpose model should be solving end to end yet.

And the last piece, which I think gets underweighted, is evaluation. For these harder modalities, the ground truth is often expensive or ambiguous. So whatever architectural choice you make, you need clinicians in the loop assessing whether the model's reasoning about that data actually holds up, not just whether it hits a benchmark number. That's been true in every modality we've worked on, and I don't think it goes away as the models get better.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the model doesn’t necessarily need to ingest every modality directly. Some biomedical data might be better handled by a specialized tool or model, and the general-purpose model can learn when to use that tool, what questions to ask of it, and how to interpret the result.

You can imagine a system where a language model coordinates several specialized components. The important thing is preserving enough information—and enough of the uncertainty—that it can reason responsibly about what those components return. If you turn a complex measurement into a single confident sentence, you may lose exactly the detail that matters.

So I’d keep both approaches open: learning to handle more modalities directly, while also getting much better at using tools for the ones that remain difficult. Ultimately, the test is whether the whole system can answer a meaningful biomedical question reliably.

r004.rationale: It supports both direct handling and tool use for modalities that remain difficult, but does not clearly predict combining tool-mediated analysis with direct modality encoding in modality-dependent ways.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to ask what information you need from that modality and how you can preserve it in a form the model can use. Some biomedical data may be difficult to feed directly into a general-purpose model, but that doesn’t mean you should ignore it—or assume that converting everything to text is sufficient.

One approach is to use specialized tools or encoders that understand the modality, and let the model work with those. The important question then is whether that interface preserves the information needed for the clinical task. You want to evaluate the whole system on that task, because a representation that looks reasonable can still discard something clinically important.
